title: SQL 100-Mark Professional Mock Examination (Test 1)
description: Comprehensive 5-section examination covering Fundamentals (20 marks), Debugging (15 marks), Technical Problem Solving (25 marks), Practical Implementation (25 marks), and System Architecture (15 marks). Total: 100 marks.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What is the primary distinction between WHERE and HAVING clauses in SQL?

options.text: HAVING can only inspect indexed primary key columns
WHERE executes after ORDER BY to sort final results
HAVING modifies underlying table schemas while WHERE is read-only
WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters grouped rows after aggregation

questions.explanation: SQL evaluates WHERE prior to GROUP BY aggregation, whereas HAVING filters aggregate buckets post-grouping.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which JOIN preserves all rows from the left table and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL?

options.text: CROSS JOIN
NATURAL INTERSECT
LEFT OUTER JOIN
INNER JOIN

questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table along with matching rows from the right table, yielding NULL when no match exists.

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which properties make up the four ACID guarantees in relational databases?

options.text: Durability
Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation

questions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent independence), and Durability (persisted commits).
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What data structure do most relational databases use by default for standard table indexes?

options.text: Balanced B-Tree (or B+Tree) supporting O(log n) lookups and range scans
Singly linked list scanning O(n) sequential nodes
Unindexed CSV append buffer
FIFO ring queue

questions.explanation: B+Trees keep keys sorted in shallow hierarchical pages, accelerating equality lookups and range filters (BETWEEN, >, <).
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What condition is violated if a non-key column depends on only part of a composite primary key?

options.text: First Normal Form (1NF)
Entity Nullability Constraint
Referential Trigger Integrity
Second Normal Form (2NF)

questions.explanation: 2NF requires being in 1NF and eliminating partial dependencies on a composite primary key.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which SQL window function assigns consecutive integers without skipping ranks when ties occur?

options.text: ROW_NUMBER()
NTILE(1)
DENSE_RANK()
RANK()

questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK() assigns identical ranks to tied rows and increments the next rank by 1 (e.g., 1, 1, 2), whereas RANK() skips (1, 1, 3).
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What happens if an aggregate function like SUM(bonus) encounters NULL values in some rows?

options.text: NULL values are coerced into -1 automatically
SQL aggregate functions ignore NULL values except COUNT(*)
SUM always returns 0 as soon as one NULL is encountered
SUM raises a DivisionByNull runtime error

questions.explanation: Aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) ignore NULL entries, whereas COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Which statements about FOREIGN KEY constraints are true?

options.text: They enforce referential integrity between child and parent tables
ON DELETE CASCADE deletes dependent child rows when the referenced parent row is removed
They require a matching candidate key (PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE) in the referenced table
They automatically duplicate all parent columns into the child table

questions.explanation: Foreign keys preserve referential integrity against a parent PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE column and support ON DELETE/UPDATE actions.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: Why does COUNT(*) behave differently from COUNT(email) on an orders table?

options.text: COUNT(email) automatically deduplicates distinct email strings
COUNT(*) is invalid ANSI SQL syntax
COUNT(email) sorts the table alphabetically first
COUNT(*) counts total rows regardless of NULLs; COUNT(email) only counts rows where email IS NOT NULL

questions.explanation: COUNT(column) skips rows with NULL values in that specific column, while COUNT(*) counts every row matched.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: What does UNION do differently from UNION ALL when combining two SELECT results?

options.text: UNION ignores mismatched column counts
UNION ALL automatically creates a temporary disk table
UNION deduplicates identical result rows; UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates without a sort/hash step
UNION ALL performs an inner join on matching IDs

questions.explanation: UNION removes duplicate rows (costing a distinct sort/hash), while UNION ALL appends results directly and is faster when duplicates are acceptable.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Why will the following SQL query fail to execute on strict ANSI SQL engines?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT department_id, first_name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;

options.text: COUNT(*) cannot be paired with GROUP BY
Trailing semicolons are invalid inside SELECT queries
The FROM clause must precede the SELECT clause
`first_name` is in the SELECT list without being aggregated or included in GROUP BY

questions.explanation: Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT projection must appear in the GROUP BY clause to preserve deterministic grouping.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Why does a query filtering `WHERE email != 'admin@site.com'` accidentally exclude rows where `email` is NULL?

options.text: The `!=` operator is ignored on VARCHAR columns
Database optimizers automatically drop rows containing NULLs on table creation
In SQL three-valued logic, comparing any value to NULL with `!=` yields UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as false
NULL evaluates to equal `'admin@site.com'` internally

questions.explanation: Three-valued logic requires explicit `OR email IS NULL` or `IS DISTINCT FROM` when preserving NULL entries.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Why does wrapping an indexed column like `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` prevent B-Tree index usage?
questions.codeSnippet: SELECT id FROM invoices WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026;

options.text: Created timestamps cannot be indexed with B-Trees
Applying a function to the indexed column breaks sargability, forcing a sequential scan unless rewritten as a date range
SQL engines forbid integers in WHERE predicates
YEAR() locks the table exclusively

questions.explanation: Non-sargable predicates (`YEAR(created_at)`) force evaluation on every row. Rewrite as `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'`.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Notice this query converts a LEFT JOIN accidentally into an INNER JOIN. Which line causes the defect?
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

options.text: `WHERE o.status = 'paid'` filters out unmatched NULL right-table rows; moving that predicate into the `ON` clause preserves unmatched customers
LEFT JOIN must use RIGHT OUTER syntax instead
The SELECT alias `o.total` breaks NULL propagation
Customers cannot be joined to orders on an integer ID

questions.explanation: Filtering a nullable right-table column in WHERE drops unmatched NULL rows. Place the condition inside the JOIN ... ON predicate instead.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Given rows with scores [90, 90, 80], what sequence does `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)` return?
questions.explanation: RANK() leaves gaps after ties (1, 1, 3), while DENSE_RANK() emits (1, 1, 2) and ROW_NUMBER() emits (1, 2, 3).
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: An analytical report joins 50 million `events` rows with `users`, scanning the full `events` table on every run. What creates the largest speedup?

options.text: Convert primary keys from BIGINT to UUID strings across all partitions
Remove all indexes so PostgreSQL scans disk sequentially without memory overhead
Wrap every column in `LOWER(TRIM(...))` inside the WHERE clause
Create a composite index matching the high-selectivity filter and join key, and replace `SELECT *` with explicit needed columns

questions.explanation: Targeted composite indexes (e.g., `(user_id, created_at)`) and covering projections cut disk I/O dramatically.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: You need the single most recent order per customer without running correlated subqueries for each row. Which SQL pattern solves this cleanly?

options.text: Select all orders into client memory and sort with Python
Add DISTINCT on created_at globally without PARTITION BY
Use a CTE with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and filter `WHERE rn = 1`
Run SELECT MAX(id) inside an unindexed cross join

questions.explanation: Top-N per group via `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` computes in a single indexed pass or sort without correlated re-scans.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: A billing transfer updates two rows inside concurrent requests, occasionally deadlocking when locks are acquired in opposite order. How do you prevent deadlocks?

options.text: Increase statement timeout to 24 hours
Acquire row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) in a consistent canonical key ordering across all transactions
Drop transaction isolation down to READ UNCOMMITTED
Remove COMMIT statements and rely on autocommit per row

questions.explanation: Consistent lock ordering breaks circular wait conditions, preventing classic two-transaction deadlocks while retaining strict SERIALIZABLE/REPEATABLE safety.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: An `OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20` pagination query degrades severely on deep pages. What replacement scales in O(log n) regardless of page depth?

options.text: Keyset (seek) pagination filtering `WHERE created_at < :last_seen_ts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`
Wrapping OFFSET in two nested CTEs
Increasing shared_buffers by 50MB without index changes
Sorting in ascending and descending order simultaneously

questions.explanation: Keyset pagination jumps straight into the B-Tree index via the cursor key, avoiding discarding hundreds of thousands of preceding rows.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: How do you inspect why a PostgreSQL query runs slow and verify whether an index or sequential scan was chosen at runtime?

options.text: Inspect database migration filenames manually
Use `SHOW COLUMNS` on the parent schema
Ping the TCP database port with ICMP packets
Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the query inside a rolled-back read transaction

questions.explanation: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the plan (when safe or rolled back) showing actual vs estimated rows, buffer hits, and exact join algorithms.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Complete the Common Table Expression (CTE) to compute a running cumulative revenue ordered by `order_date`:

options.text: GROUP BY order_date
HAVING order_date > 0
JOIN daily_sales ON order_date
ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

questions.explanation: Specifying `ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` calculates a deterministic running total.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Write an idempotent upsert in PostgreSQL when inserting a user score into `enrollments(student_id, course_slug, score)` with a UNIQUE `(student_id, course_slug)` key:

options.text: INSERT IGNORE ALL INTO enrollments VALUES (...);
SELECT OR INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO enrollments (...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (student_id, course_slug) DO UPDATE SET score = EXCLUDED.score;
DROP TABLE enrollments; INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (...);

questions.explanation: `ON CONFLICT (...) DO UPDATE` atomically updates existing rows or inserts new ones without race conditions.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: How should an API backend execute user-supplied search input inside a SQL query to guarantee zero SQL injection risk?

options.text: Disable WHERE clauses when user strings contain spaces
Use parameterized prepared statements (`SELECT * FROM courses WHERE title ILIKE $1`, [`%${term}%`])
Interpolate the string after stripping single quotes via JavaScript `.replace("'", "")`
Base64-encode the whole SQL statement before sending it over HTTP

questions.explanation: Prepared statements bind values cleanly as protocol parameters separate from SQL syntax parsing, neutralizing SQL injection.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: How do you safely execute a ledger transfer where debiting account A and crediting account B must either both commit or both rollback?

options.text: Wrap both UPDATEs inside `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;` checking `balance >= amount`, rolling back on error (`ROLLBACK;`)
Execute two unrelated HTTP calls sequentially without locking
Store negative numbers inside a VARCHAR column and recalculate daily
Disable foreign key constraints before UPDATE

questions.explanation: Explicit SQL transactions preserve atomicity and consistency across multi-statement financial mutations.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Which partial index best optimizes querying only active pending background jobs from a 10M-row table where 99.8% are `completed`?

options.text: CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_completed ON jobs(payload_json);
CREATE TABLE jobs_all AS SELECT * FROM jobs;
ALTER TABLE jobs DROP PRIMARY KEY;
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_pending ON jobs(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

questions.explanation: A partial index (`WHERE status = 'pending'`) stays tiny (indexing just 0.2% of rows) and speeds worker queue polling dramatically.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: Read-heavy analytics dashboards overload the transactional primary PostgreSQL database. What architectural scaling pattern isolates read load cleanly?

options.text: Disable ACID durability (`fsync=off`) on the primary production database
Allow browser clients to connect directly over public port 5432 without pooling
Delete all historical rows older than 24 hours automatically
Provision asynchronous streaming read replicas for heavy analytics/reporting queries and route OLTP writes to the primary

questions.explanation: Read replicas absorb reporting and BI scans while keeping write-heavy primary OLTP response times low and predictable.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: A serverless backend spawns 1,500 short-lived worker instances during peak spikes, exhausting PostgreSQL max_connections. What component fixes this?

options.text: Raise max_connections to 50,000 on a 2GB RAM node
Drop all secondary indexes
Place a connection pooler (PgBouncer in transaction mode / Supabase Supavisor) in front of PostgreSQL
Restart PostgreSQL every 60 seconds via cron

questions.explanation: Transaction-mode connection pooling multiplexes thousands of ephemeral serverless connections across a bounded pool of server backends.
questions.recommendedLessonTitle: Core Primitives and Syntax in SQL

questions.prompt: You need zero-downtime schema evolution when renaming or replacing a heavily used column in production. What strategy avoids breaking running pods?

options.text: Store all fields inside one single comma-delimited text column
Use the Expand-Contract pattern: add the new column + dual-write/backfill -> switch application reads -> drop old column safely
Run ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN during peak traffic without updating app code first
Drop the table and re-import from backup while live users browse

questions.explanation: Expand-Contract migrations keep both old and new schemas compatible across rolling deployments, guaranteeing zero downtime.
